'''''Ceratophyllum demersum''''', commonly called '''hornwort''' or '''coontail''',<ref name="issg-ecology" /> is a species of flowering plant in the genus ''[[Ceratophyllum]]''. ''Ceratophyllum demersum'' is a submerged, free-floating aquatic plant, with a cosmopolitan distribution, native to all continents except Antarctica. It is a harmful weed introduced in New Zealand.<ref name="issg-ecology">[http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=281&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN Ceratophyllum demersum] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160326094021/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=281&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN |date=2016-03-26 }} on the Global Invasive Species database (2006).</ref> It is also a popular aquarium plant. Its genome has been sequenced to study angiosperm evolution.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Yongzhi |last2=Sun |first2=Pengchuan |last3=Lv |first3=Leke |last4=Wang |first4=Donglei |last5=Ru |first5=Dafu |last6=Li |first6=Ying |last7=Ma |first7=Tao |last8=Zhang |first8=Lei |last9=Shen |first9=Xingxing |last10=Meng |first10=Fanbo |last11=Jiao |first11=Beibei |last12=Shan |first12=Lanxing |last13=Liu |first13=Man |last14=Wang |first14=Qingfeng |last15=Qin |first15=Zhiji |date=2020 |title=Prickly waterlily and rigid hornwort genomes shed light on early angiosperm evolution |journal=Nature Plants |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=215–222 |doi=10.1038/s41477-020-0594-6 |issn=2055-0278 |pmc=8075997 |pmid=32094642}}</ref>

==Name==
The genus name ''Ceratophyllum'' is latinized from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] κέρας ''kéras'' (combining κέρατ- ''kerat-''), "horn, antler", and φύλλον ''phúllon'', "leaf", in allusion to the resemblance of the leaves to antlers.<ref>{{Citation |last=Roy |first=Bruce |year=2004 |title=An Illustrated Guide to Common Weeds of New Zealand |publisher=New Zealand Plant Protection Society |publication-place= |page=133 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/An_Illustrated_Guide_to_Common_Weeds_of/J1smAQAAMAAJ |access-date=}}</ref> This name is directly mirrored in the [[German language|German]] and [[Dutch language|Dutch]] common names, ''Hornblatt'' and ''hoornblad'' respectively.

In English the plant is most commonly called '''hornwort''', a name shared with the unrelated [[Anthocerotophyta|Anthocerotophytes]] (which has a distinctive horn-like [[sporophyte]]); for this reason, the name '''coontail''' (or '''coon's tail''') is sometimes preferred.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}} Other common names include '''hornweed''', '''morassweed''', '''cornifle''', and  '''hornleaf'''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Schaffner |first=John H. |author-link=
John Henry Schaffner |date=1928 |title=Field Manual of the Flora of Ohio and Adjacent Territory |publisher=R. G. Adams & Company |location=Columbus, Ohio |isbn= |pages=211–212 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Field_Manual_of_the_Flora_of_Ohio_and_Ad/YafwAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA211 |access-date=}}</ref>

==Description==
An aquatic plant, ''Ceratophyllum demersum'' has stems that reach lengths of {{convert|1|–|3|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}}, with numerous side shoots making a single specimen appear as a large, bushy mass. The leaves are produced in whorls of six to twelve, each leaf 8–40 mm long, simple, or forked into two to eight thread-like segments edged with spiny teeth; they are stiff and brittle. It is [[plant sexuality|monoecious]], with separate male and female flowers produced on the same plant. The flowers are small, 2 mm long, with eight or more greenish-brown petals; they are produced in the leaf axils. The fruit is a small nut 4–5 mm long, usually with three spines, two [[Anatomical terms of location#Elongated organisms with distinctive ends|basal]] and one [[Anatomical terms of location#Elongated organisms with distinctive ends|apical]], 1–12 mm long. Plants with the two basal nut spines very short are sometimes distinguished as ''Ceratophyllum demersum'' var. ''apiculatum'' (Cham.) Asch., and those with no basal spines sometimes distinguished as ''Ceratophyllum demersum'' var. ''inerme'' Gay ex Radcl.-Sm.<ref name=foc>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200007091 ''Ceratophyllum demersum'']</ref><ref name=fna>Flora of North America: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200007091 ''Ceratophyllum demersum'']</ref><ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20070621080912/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=1600|title=''Ceratophyllum demersum''}}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref> It can form [[turion (botany)|turions]]: buds that sink to the bottom of the water and stay there during the winter before forming new plants in spring.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

==Identification==
Rigid coontails can be easily confused with [[soft hornwort|soft coontails]] (''Ceratophyllum submersum''), especially when there is young growth with less stiff leaves. A key feature to look out for is the number of times a leaf is branched: the leaves are only forked once or twice, rather than three to four times in soft coontails. They are also rather more roughly toothed.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Ceratophyllum demersum s. str. sl3.jpg|thumb|The leaves are forked only twice in rigid coontails.]]

==Distribution and habitat==
''Ceratophyllum demersum'' grows in lakes, ponds, and quiet streams with summer water temperatures of 15–30 °C{{citation needed|date=October 2011}} and a rich nutrient status. In North America, it occurs in the entire US and Canada, except [[Newfoundland and Labrador|Newfoundland]].<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=CEDE4 USDA PLANTS database on C. demersum] as of 2011.</ref> In Europe, it has been reported as far north as at a latitude of 66 degrees in Norway.<ref>[http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution_display.asp?si=281&ri=18427&pc=*&sts=&status=Alien&lang=EN#Alien ISSG database, reports in Norway] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160328140659/http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution_display.asp?si=281&ri=18427&pc=*&sts=&status=Alien&lang=EN#Alien |date=2016-03-28 }} (based on Mjelde, 1997)</ref> Other reported occurrences include China, [[Siberia]] (at 66 degrees North), [[Burkina Faso]] and in the [[Volta River]] in Ghana (Africa), Vietnam, and New Zealand (introduced).<ref name="issg-distrib">[http://www.issg.org/database/species/distribution.asp?si=281&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN ISSG: distribution of C. demersum]</ref> ''Ceratophyllum demersum'' grows in still or very slow-moving water.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

===Invasive status===
Coontails are a declared weed under the Tasmanian Weed Management Act 1999 in Tasmania, Australia,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dpiw.tas.gov.au/inter,nsf/WebPages/LBUN-87B7WC |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121127141357/http://www.dpiw.tas.gov.au/inter,nsf/WebPages/LBUN-87B7WC |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 27, 2012 |title=Hornwort| publisher= Department of Primary Industries, Parks, Water and Environment| accessdate=21 September 2012}}</ref> and is classed as an unwanted organism in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Hornwort| publisher = MPI Biosecurity New Zealand| date = 29 May 2012| accessdate = 2012-09-21| url = http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/hornwort| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121205035215/http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/hornwort| archive-date = 5 December 2012| url-status = dead| df = dmy-all}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''C. demersum'' has [[allelopathic]] qualities as it excretes substances that inhibit the growth of [[phytoplankton]] and [[cyanobacteria]] (blue-green algae).<ref name="issg-ecology"/><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.thekrib.com/Plants/Algae/cyanobacteria.html#4 |title = Cyanobacteria (Blue-green Algae)}}</ref> Its dense growth can outcompete other underwater vegetation, leading to loss of biodiversity. In New Zealand, it has caused problems with hydroelectric power plants.<ref name="issg-ecology"/>

==Cultivation and uses==
This species is often used as a floating freshwater plant in both coldwater and tropical aquaria. Though without roots, it may attach itself to the [[Substrate (aquarium)|substrate]] or objects in the aquarium. Its fluffy, filamentous, bright-green leaves provide excellent cover for newly hatched fish. It is propagated by cuttings.<ref name=hiscock>Hiscock, P. (2003). ''Encyclopedia of Aquarium Plants''. Interpret Publishing, United States and Canada {{ISBN|0-7641-5521-0}}.</ref> This plant appears to drop all its leaves when exposed to products designed to kill snails. The stems can recover relatively quickly, growing new leaves within a few weeks.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

It is frequently used as a model organism for studies of plant physiology.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=ceratophyllum&hl=en&as_sdt=0&as_vis=1 |title = Google Scholar}}</ref> One of the reasons for this is that it allows studies on shoot effects without influence of a root, which often makes interpretation of nutrition and toxicity experiments difficult in terrestrial plants. As it is free floating and therefore does not require a solid substrate, it has been used successfully in the biological life support systems "Aquarack/CEBAS" and "Omegahab" on space flights.<ref>Blüm V, Stretzke E, Kreuzberg K (1994) CEBAS-aquarack project – the mini-module as tool in artificial ecosystem research. Acta Astronautica 33: 167–177</ref><ref>Voeste D, Levine LH, Levine HG, Blüm V (2003) Pigment composition and concentrations within the plant (Ceratophyllum demersum L.) component of the STS-89 C.E.B.A.S. Mini-Module spaceflight experiment.  Advances in Space Research  31, 211-214</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.russianspaceweb.com/bion_m_landing.html |title=Landing of Bion-M No. 1 satellite |accessdate=2013-05-20 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130609050748/http://www.russianspaceweb.com/bion_m_landing.html |archivedate=2013-06-09 }}</ref> 

Coontail plants or the epiphytes they support have been shown to degrade the herbicide atrazine.<ref>Rupassara, S. I., R.A. Larson, G.K. Sims, and K.A. Marley. 2002 Degradation of atrazine by hornwort in aquatic systems. Bioremediation Journal 6(3): 217-224.</ref>
